lead: Every power switch loses energy in two ways: its drop while it conducts (conduction loss) and a burst of heat at each turn-on and turn-off while voltage and current overlap (switching loss), which grows with frequency. All the heat flows from the junction through the case and heat sink to the air, each step with a thermal resistance. Thermal design picks the heat sink that keeps the junction below its limit on the hottest day.
prereq: You need: the turn-on and turn-off intervals of the MOSFET and IGBT chapter.

blocks.text: During a transition the switch has both a large voltage and a large current, and their product is power. The energy of one transition depends on how v and i change. With a clamped inductive load (the usual case in choppers and inverters, with a freewheeling diode), the current changes first at full voltage, then the voltage changes at full current, so each transition is a triangle of power with peak V I. With a resistive load, voltage and current change together, and the energy is a third as large.
Esw = ½ V I tsw (inductive), Esw = V I tsw / 6 (resistive)
where E<sub>sw</sub> is the energy of one transition (J), V the blocking voltage (V), I the on-state current (A) and t<sub>sw</sub> the transition time (s).

the average switching loss with an inductive load, in watts, where t<sub>on</sub> and t<sub>off</sub> are the turn-on and turn-off transition times (s) and f<sub>s</sub> the switching frequency (Hz). Datasheets often give E<sub>on</sub> and E<sub>off</sub> directly at a test voltage and current; then P<sub>sw</sub> = (E<sub>on</sub> + E<sub>off</sub>) f<sub>s</sub>.
Shorter transitions cut the loss; at fixed transition times, P<sub>sw</sub> is proportional to f<sub>s</sub>.

While on, a diode, thyristor, BJT or IGBT drops a roughly constant voltage, so P<sub>cond</sub> = V<sub>on</sub> I D, where I is the current while conducting and D the fraction of the period it conducts. A MOSFET is a resistance, so P<sub>cond</sub> = I² R<sub>DS(on)</sub> D. If the current given is already the average or rms over the whole period, D is already included and must not be applied again. The total device loss is P = P<sub>cond</sub> + P<sub>sw</sub>; use the worst-case current and the hot value of R<sub>DS(on)</sub> or V<sub>on</sub>.

blocks.where: the total heat the cooling path must remove, in watts.

blocks.text: Heat flows from the junction to the case, across the mounting interface to the heat sink, and from the sink to the ambient air. Each step has a thermal resistance in °C/W: Rθ<sub>JC</sub> (junction to case, from the datasheet), Rθ<sub>CS</sub> (case to sink, set by the pad or grease and the mounting pressure) and Rθ<sub>SA</sub> (sink to ambient, from the heat-sink maker). They are in series, like resistors carrying the heat flow P, and temperature plays the role of voltage.
where T<sub>j</sub> is the junction temperature and T<sub>a</sub> the ambient temperature (°C), P the total loss (W) and each Rθ in °C/W.

To choose a heat sink, rearrange: Rθ<sub>SA</sub> ≤ (T<sub>j,max</sub> − T<sub>a</sub>)/P − Rθ<sub>JC</sub> − Rθ<sub>CS</sub>. A lower Rθ<sub>SA</sub> means a bigger sink, more fins or forced air. For short pulses the junction does not reach the steady value, because the die and case store heat; datasheets give the transient thermal impedance Zθ<sub>JC(t)</sub>, which is smaller than Rθ<sub>JC</sub> for short pulses.

examples.question: An IGBT in a chopper switches 10 A off and on against 200 V at 10 kHz, with an inductive load. Its turn-on time is 1 µs and turn-off time 2 µs. It conducts for half of each period with V<sub>CE(sat)</sub> = 2 V. Rθ<sub>JC</sub> = 1.0 °C/W, Rθ<sub>CS</sub> = 0.5 °C/W, T<sub>a</sub> = 40 °C and T<sub>j,max</sub> = 125 °C. Find the total loss and the largest heat-sink resistance allowed. A 0.6 °C/W sink is chosen; find T<sub>j</sub> and the case and sink temperatures.
steps: Switching energy per cycle: ½ × 200 × 10 × (1 + 2) × 10<sup>−6</sup> = 3 × 10<sup>−3</sup> J; P<sub>sw</sub> = 3 mJ × 10 000 Hz = 30 W.
Conduction loss: P<sub>cond</sub> = 2 V × 10 A × 0.5 = 10 W. Total P = 30 + 10 = 40 W.
Down the path: T<sub>case</sub> = 124 − 40 × 1.0 = 84 °C; T<sub>sink</sub> = 84 − 40 × 0.5 = 64 °C; and 64 − 40 × 0.6 = 40 °C, the ambient.
examples.answer: P = 40 W (30 W switching, 10 W conduction); Rθ<sub>SA</sub> ≤ 0.625 °C/W; with 0.6 °C/W, T<sub>j</sub> = 124 °C, T<sub>case</sub> = 84 °C, T<sub>sink</sub> = 64 °C.

examples.question: The same 200 V, 10 A transitions (1 µs on, 2 µs off) at 10 kHz switch a resistive load instead. Find the switching loss and compare it with the inductive case.
steps: Energy per cycle with linear, simultaneous changes: V I (t<sub>on</sub> + t<sub>off</sub>) / 6 = 200 × 10 × 3 × 10<sup>−6</sup> ÷ 6 = 1 × 10<sup>−3</sup> J.
Ratio: 30 W ÷ 10 W = 3. With a resistive load the current falls as the voltage rises, so the power peak is only V I / 4 and the energy a third of the inductive case.
examples.answer: 10 W, one third of the 30 W found with the inductive load.

traps: Leaving out t<sub>off</sub>: with t<sub>on</sub> = 1 µs and t<sub>off</sub> = 2 µs that gives 10 W instead of 30 W, a third of the answer.
Using the resistive factor 1/6 for an inductive (freewheeling-diode) load; it under-reads P<sub>sw</sub> by a factor of 3.
Putting f<sub>s</sub> in kHz: 10 kHz is 10 000 Hz; the answer comes out 1000 times too small.
Thermal resistances of one path are in series and add; they are not combined like parallel resistors.
A lower Rθ<sub>SA</sub> means a bigger heat sink, not a smaller one.

quiz.q: Write the switching-loss formula for an inductive load and define each symbol.
quiz.a: P<sub>sw</sub> = ½ V I (t<sub>on</sub> + t<sub>off</sub>) f<sub>s</sub>: V blocking voltage, I on-state current, t<sub>on</sub> and t<sub>off</sub> transition times, f<sub>s</sub> switching frequency.

quiz.q: Name the three thermal resistances from junction to ambient.
quiz.a: Junction-to-case Rθ<sub>JC</sub>, case-to-sink Rθ<sub>CS</sub> and sink-to-ambient Rθ<sub>SA</sub>.

quiz.q: Why does switching loss rise in proportion to frequency?
quiz.a: Each cycle has one turn-on and one turn-off with fixed energy; more cycles per second means proportionally more energy per second.

quiz.q: A switch has V = 100 V, I = 5 A, t<sub>on</sub> = 2 µs, t<sub>off</sub> = 1 µs and f<sub>s</sub> = 20 kHz with an inductive load. Find P<sub>sw</sub>.
In the worked example, the heat sink is changed to 1.0 °C/W. Find T<sub>j</sub> and say whether it is safe.
quiz.a: T<sub>j</sub> = 40 + 40 × (1.0 + 0.5 + 1.0) = 140 °C, above the 125 °C limit: not safe.

quiz.q: A datasheet gives Rθ<sub>JC</sub> = 1.5 °C/W, Rθ<sub>CS</sub> = 0.4 °C/W and the sink is 2.0 °C/W. With T<sub>a</sub> = 45 °C and P = 20 W, is T<sub>j</sub> below 120 °C?
A designer doubles f<sub>s</sub>, keeping everything else fixed. What happens to the losses and the heat sink of the worked example?
quiz.a: P<sub>sw</sub> doubles to 60 W, P<sub>cond</sub> stays 10 W, so P = 70 W. Allowed total resistance = 85 ÷ 70 = 1.214 °C/W, so Rθ<sub>SA</sub> ≤ 1.214 − 1.5, a negative number: no heat sink can do it. The device must be changed, the switching made faster, or the frequency kept down.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real designs read E<sub>on</sub> and E<sub>off</sub> from datasheet curves at the actual voltage, current and temperature. Electric-vehicle inverters use liquid-cooled baseplates, and the thermal cycling of solder and bond wires sets their life. Search for ‘transient thermal impedance curve’ and ‘power module thermal cycling’.
